tips.title: Francophone means French-speaking
tips.body: **Francophone** describes a person or a place where French is spoken — *un pays francophone*, *une ville francophone*. **La Francophonie** is the family of those countries. Around **300 million** people speak French, on five continents, and most of them are not in France.

tips.title: Countries take en, au or aux
tips.body: Feminine countries take **en**: *en France, en Belgique, en Suisse*. Masculine ones take **au**: *au Canada, au Sénégal, au Maroc*. Plurals take **aux**: *aux Antilles*. The article decides the preposition, so learn each country with its gender.

tips.title: Avoir lieu is how events happen
tips.body: To say when or where an event takes place, use **avoir lieu**: *le festival a lieu en mai*, *le carnaval a lieu à Québec*. It is far more natural than *est* and it is what texts use — so spotting it in a reading passage tells you a date or a place is coming.

tips.title: Dates: le + number, and no capital on months
tips.body: French dates are **le** + the number + the month, with no *of*: *le 20 mars*, *le 14 juillet*. Months and days take **no capital letter**. The one exception is the first of the month: *le premier mai*, never *le un mai*.

tips.title: Reading a text about an event: hunt for the four Ws
tips.body: Any text about an event answers **what**, **when**, **where** and **what happens**. Find the name, then a month or date, then a place after *à* or *en*, then the verbs — *on peut voir, il y a, on écoute*. Those four answer most comprehension questions before you have read every word.

steps.title: Le monde francophone
steps.body:
French is spoken far beyond France. Around **300 million** people speak it, across **Europe**, **Africa**, **North America**, the **Caribbean** and the **Pacific** — and a Year 9 reading text is as likely to be set in Dakar or Montréal as in Paris.

**Francophone** is the word for it: *un pays francophone* is a French-speaking country, and **la Francophonie** is the group of those countries together. Being able to name some of them, with the right preposition, is the vocabulary this topic starts from.

**Europe**: *la France, la Belgique, la Suisse, le Luxembourg, Monaco*.

**Afrique**: *le Sénégal, la Côte d'Ivoire, le Maroc, l'Algérie, la Tunisie, Madagascar*.

**Amérique et Caraïbes**: *le Canada* (above all *le Québec*), *Haïti, la Guadeloupe, la Martinique*.

**Océan Indien et Pacifique**: *la Réunion, Tahiti, la Nouvelle-Calédonie*.

The preposition for **in** depends on the country's gender: **en** for feminine countries, **au** for masculine, **aux** for plurals — *en France, au Canada, aux Antilles*. Cities take **à**: *à Dakar, à Montréal*.

steps.title: Les grands événements
steps.body:
Four events come up again and again in textbooks and exam texts, because each one says something about where French is spoken and what people there do together.

**la Journée internationale de la Francophonie** — **le 20 mars**, dans le monde entier. Concerts, films et concours pour fêter la langue française. It is the day the French-speaking world celebrates having a language in common.

**le Festival de Cannes** — **en mai**, à Cannes, en France. Un festival de cinéma; le meilleur film gagne la Palme d'Or.

**le Tour de France** — **en juillet**, en France, avec l'arrivée à Paris. Une course cycliste de trois semaines, watched on television across the world.

**le Carnaval de Québec** — **en hiver, en janvier et février**, à Québec, au Canada. Des défilés dans la neige, avec le Bonhomme Carnaval.

Notice the verb that carries all of this: **avoir lieu**, *to take place*. *Le Tour de France a lieu en juillet. Le carnaval a lieu à Québec.* In a reading text, *a lieu* is the signal that a **date or a place** is about to follow.

The traditional French calendar of *fêtes* — Epiphany, la Chandeleur, le 14 juillet — is covered in the topic **Festivals and traditions**; this one is about the events that gather the whole Francophone world.

steps.title: Describing an event in the present
steps.body:
To describe an event you need three things: **when and where** it happens, **what there is** to see, and **what people do**. Each has a small set of phrases that do most of the work.

**When and where**: *a lieu* + a month or a place. *Le festival a lieu en mai, à Cannes.*

**What there is**: **il y a** — *there is / there are*. *Il y a des concerts, il y a un défilé, il y a beaucoup de monde.* One phrase, no agreement, and it never changes.

**What people can do**: **on peut** + infinitive — *you can*. *On peut voir des films. On peut écouter de la musique. On peut danser dans la rue.* The verb after *on peut* stays in the **infinitive**.

**What people do**: the present tense with **on**, which French uses for *we* and *people* alike. *On regarde, on mange, on chante.* With *on* the verb takes the **il / elle** form, which for **-er** verbs is the stem plus **-e**.

The verb **avoir** is worth having in full here, because *il y a* and *a lieu* both come from it, and because *j'ai* will carry the perfect tense later this term.

steps.title: Reading a text about an event
steps.body:
Reading texts about events look harder than they are, because they are full of names and numbers. Those are exactly what the questions ask for, so the trick is to **hunt for the four Ws** rather than translate every word.

**What?** The **name** of the event, usually with *le festival de…*, *la fête de…*, *le carnaval de…*.

**When?** A **month** (*en juillet*), a **date** (*le 20 mars*), a **season** (*en hiver*) or a frequency (*chaque année*, *tous les quatre ans*). Months take no capital letter, which makes them easy to miss — so scan for *janvier, février, mars…*

**Where?** A place after **à** (a city) or **en / au** (a country).

**What happens?** Look for **il y a**, **on peut** and present-tense verbs with **on**.

Then the **cognates** — words that look like English and mean the same: *festival, concert, cinéma, musique, sport, artiste, international, célèbre*. A text about an event is often half cognates.

**Two traps.** *Assister à* means **to attend**, not *to assist*. And *gagner* means **to win** (or to earn), so *elle a gagné la Palme d'Or* is a winner, not a gainer.

visuals.problem: Text: "Chaque année, en mai, le Festival de Cannes a lieu sur la Côte d'Azur. Pendant douze jours, on peut voir des films du monde entier et il y a beaucoup de stars. Le meilleur film gagne la Palme d'Or." Answer: when, where, how long, and what wins.

steps.text: **When**: *chaque année, en mai* — every year, in May
steps.note: two time phrases in a row: the frequency, then the month

steps.text: **Where**: *sur la Côte d'Azur* — on the Riviera; *Cannes* is in the name
steps.note: the place is after sur here, not à — read the preposition you are given

steps.text: **How long**: *pendant douze jours* — for twelve days
steps.note: pendant + a length of time is "for"; the number is the answer

steps.text: **What wins**: *le meilleur film gagne la Palme d'Or* — the best film wins the Palme d'Or
steps.note: gagner is to win; meilleur is best

steps.text: Words you never needed to translate: *stars, films, festival* — cognates carried the sense
steps.note: read for the Ws first; the rest is confirmation

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name three Francophone countries outside Europe, each with the right word for *in*.
2. When and where does the Festival de Cannes take place?
3. What does *francophone* mean?

**Part B.**

4. Translate: *Le carnaval a lieu en hiver, à Québec.*
5. Translate into French: *There are concerts and you can dance.*
6. Write the present tense of **avoir** in full.

**Part C.**

7. Write four sentences in French about the Journée de la Francophonie: what it is, when, what there is, and your opinion.
8. Read: "Tous les quatre ans, les Jeux de la Francophonie ont lieu dans un pays francophone. Il y a des compétitions sportives et des concours artistiques." When do they happen, and what two kinds of thing are there?
9. Explain the difference between *assister à* and *participer à*, with an example of each.

For question 7, use *a lieu*, *il y a*, *on peut* and *parce que* — one each.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Use the right preposition every time.** *En* for feminine countries, *au* for masculine, *aux* for plurals, *à* for cities. *Je vais en France, au Canada, aux Antilles, à Dakar.* A wrong one is a small error that examiners see instantly; a run of right ones reads as fluent.

**Reach for avoir lieu.** *Le festival a lieu en mai* is what a French speaker writes; *le festival est en mai* is what a learner writes. The same goes for **se dérouler** — *la course se déroule en juillet* — which is worth having as a second option for range.

**Vary how you say "there is".** *Il y a* is essential, but a top answer also has *on trouve* (you find), *on peut voir* (you can see) and *il existe*. Three ways of saying the same thing is what **range of vocabulary** means on the mark scheme.

**Add duration and frequency.** *Pendant trois semaines*, *chaque année*, *tous les quatre ans*, *depuis 1903*. Numbers and time phrases are cheap to include and count as **detail**.

**Give an opinion with a reason, and a comparison.** *C'est mon événement préféré parce que…* earns; *c'est plus intéressant que le football parce que…* earns more. **Plus … que** and **moins … que** lift a description into an evaluation.

**Read for the signal, then confirm.** In comprehension, find *a lieu* for the date and place, *il y a* for what is there, *pendant* for how long, *gagner* for who wins — then read around each one. Translating the whole text is slower and no more accurate.

**Know the two false friends.** *Assister à* is **to attend** — *j'assiste au concert* means you are in the audience. *Participer à* is **to take part** — you are on the stage. Confusing them reverses the meaning of a sentence.

**Months and days take no capital.** *en juillet*, *le lundi*. Capitalising them is an English habit that marks an answer as translated rather than written.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Francophone** = French-speaking; **la Francophonie** = the French-speaking world, around **300 million** speakers.
- Countries on five continents: *la Belgique, la Suisse, le Canada, le Sénégal, le Maroc, la Côte d'Ivoire, Haïti, la Réunion*.
- **En** + feminine country, **au** + masculine, **aux** + plural, **à** + city.
- **la Journée internationale de la Francophonie** — le 20 mars.
- **le Festival de Cannes** — en mai, à Cannes, en France.
- **le Tour de France** — en juillet, three weeks.
- **le Carnaval de Québec** — en hiver, en janvier et février.
- **Avoir lieu** = to take place: *le festival a lieu en mai*.
- **Il y a** = there is / there are, and never changes.
- **On peut** + infinitive = you can.
- **On** takes the *il / elle* form of the verb.
- **Assister à** = to attend; **participer à** = to take part; **gagner** = to win.
- Read for the **four Ws**: what, when, where, what happens.
- Dates: **le** + number + month; months take **no capital**.
- Opinion + reason: *à mon avis … parce que*.

examTechnique.body:
Match the preposition to the country — **en**, **au**, **aux** — and **à** for cities. Use **avoir lieu** for when and where an event happens, **il y a** for what is there, and **on peut** + infinitive for what you can do.

When reading, hunt for the **four Ws** and the signal words around them rather than translating everything. Give every opinion a **reason**.
examinerErrors: Using en with a masculine country, or à with a country.
Writing est instead of a lieu for an event.
Conjugating the verb after on peut.
Translating assister à as to assist.
Giving an opinion with no reason.
Missing an article before a noun.
Translating a text word by word instead of reading for the four Ws.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses **en, au, aux** and **à** correctly without hesitation, reaches for **avoir lieu** and **se dérouler**, and has more than one way of saying *there is*. It includes **duration and frequency** — *pendant trois semaines, chaque année* — as easy detail, and turns its opinion into an evaluation with **plus … que** and **parce que**. In reading it finds the signal words first and reads around them, and it never falls for *assister à*. Its months have no capitals and its nouns have their articles.
